# Capacity Network Design {.unnumbered}

A greedy algorithm to prescribe an optimal geographic allocation of blood donation appointments (slots), given competing operational objectives

# Overview

## Themes / Analytical methods

_Prescriptive analytics, Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis, Computational statistics / Numerical methods, leaflet choropleth geo-mapping, Shiny for making technical concepts accessible_

## Business Problem

### Problem Statement
The organisation's current operational setup for blood donation collection is not optimised. Appointments (slots) are not optimally distributed in either a spatial or temporal sense i.e. people who are willing and able to donate blood cannot always find a slot near them, at a suitable time. What would the collection capacity network look like if we rebuilt it from scratch in the optimal way?

### Academic Aim
A solution (likely a numerical method) that, given a set of organisational objectives along with relative weights or priorities, allocates a given number of appointments geographically, so as to maximise the likelihood of meeting those objectives.

## Scoping and planning

* I decided to consider an optimisation problem with respect to only the spatial distribution of slots, as a first step. I recognised that the temporal aspect could be dealt with independently, because I had no reason to believe that the optimal temporal distribution should be significantly different between geographical areas. As such, I established that the problem could be reduced to two independent optimisation problems, of which I would tackle the spatial one.
* I recognised this as an application for Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis (MCDA), especially considering the difficulty of expressing different organisational objectives in comparable terms e.g. collecting enough blood from Black African and Black Caribbean donors, and minimising the distance that donated blood needs to transported to manufacturing sites.

## Limitations
* Numerical methods are liable to fail to converge, or converge on a local optimum rather than a global optimum. Given their ability to approach otherwise untractable problems and compute a solution in a reasonable time, their use is justified here, as detailed below.

## Technical choices

* I recognised that the optimal solution would be a function of the ordering or weighting of the competing orgnisational objectives, and so chose to use a computational approach - an algorithm that incrementally added capacity to the next best location at each step (greedy) by using an objective function that was a weighted average of "monetised" or otherwise quantified organisational objectives.
* I decided that it was more important to be able to convey that the weighting/priority strongly determined the optimum, than it was to be able to guaranteed convergence on a contrived or otherwise arbitrary "objective" optimum. As such, I felt justified in using an approach that could sometimes miss the global optimum.
* The computational approach with the weighted objective function also allowed me to
  * demonstrate with fine control how varying the weights shifts the optimum in the direction of different extremes, to non-technical decision makers
  * compute and compare different scenarios easily
* As a proof of concept (POC), I developed a Shiny app with inputs for parameters to demonstrate the reduction of the problem to the relative weights of the competing objectives.

## Validation

As the algorithm is a simulation, there is no operational or historical data to compare its outputs with. Instead, as demonstrated in @example, a key step of the evaluation of results is to sense-check and rationalise the observations as parameters are varied and scenarios are compared. Because I wrote algorithm from first principles, and because it is deterministic, it is easy to determine evolution of the solution at iteration loop in the algorithm as necessary. It can be re-run and "paused" and examiend as desired.

## Impact  

This work enabled senior decision-makers to fully grasp the reduction of the problem into the relative weighting/ordering of organisational objectives. This was facilitated by the proof of concept Shiny app and leaflet choropleths representing the optimal solution. They allowed me to convey that there was no objective, "correct" answer to the problem, but instead that the chosen priorities, via the objective function, would allow the algorithm to prescribe a capacity allocation that would best fulfil them.

# Project code & Output

In lieu of a link to the repo, which is not public, the below explores the architecture, pseudocode, and code excerpts from the repo.

The codebase of the project consists of:

* a POC Shiny app to demonstrate the greedy algorithm
* an algorithm written in R with a more sophisticated objective function, which outputs a choropleth leaflet map for the optimal slot distribution at a constituency granularity.

# Relevance to the Senior Data Scientist role

The problem of weighing up inherently incomparable or non-monetary objectives is one that all public sector organisations face. As such, the role of computational methods and MCDA in prescriptive analytics is highly transferrable. This could include distributing resources, services, and workforce geographically, or allocating funding between them.  

# What I learnt / would improve

A key hindrance to progress was the reluctance of stakeholders to commit to a weighting/ordering of objectives. Next time, I would conduct a sensitivity analysis to understand the effect on the output (optimal allocation) that a unit change in each weight would cause. This would at least prescribe a sensible precision for the weightings, which it occured to me might make the task less daunting for decision-makers e.g. if they knew the weightings only needed to be in 10% blocks rather than 1% blocks.
